claims.text: The current additive-manufacturing baseline uses fixed laser power and a fixed scanning strategy.
Components produced by the baseline process exhibit significant thermal gradients.
The thermal gradients in the baseline process are associated with residual stresses.
The constant-power baseline has unpredictable melt-pool dynamics.
Baseline melt-pool dynamics and thermal gradients lead to inferior dimensional and mechanical properties.
Adaptive laser-power modulation will improve the dimensional precision of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Adaptive laser-power modulation will improve the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Adaptive laser-power modulation will reduce fabrication-induced defects.
Real-time temperature readings can be used to dynamically adjust laser output during layer-by-layer fabrication.
Dynamic laser-power modulation in response to temperature readings smooths the melt-pool boundary.
Dynamic laser-power modulation minimizes abrupt thermal differences.
Smoother melt-pool boundaries and smaller thermal differences produce more consistent solidification.
More consistent solidification reduces residual-stress buildup.
More consistent solidification promotes a uniform microstructure.
Reduced residual stress and a more uniform microstructure improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity.
Relative to fixed laser power, adaptive modulation is expected to increase mechanical strength.
Relative to fixed laser power, adaptive modulation is expected to reduce porosity and microcrack incidence.
The expected improvement depends on controller responsiveness and the alloy's thermal properties.
The hypothesis may not hold under extreme ambient-temperature fluctuations or for alloy compositions with radically different thermal conductivities.
